context.goal: Write concise English lessons preserving the same-whole condition and the positive-integer condition. The pages intentionally revisit the same concepts. Plan exactly ONE lesson per planning group, covering its source chunks or giving explicit omission reasons. Do not repeat full passages. Keep each board item under 80 characters. context.title: Fractions, units and necessary conditions

sources.title: Anonymous fractions source 2
sources.text: Source page 11. A fraction describes selected equal parts of the same whole. The denominator names the unit and the numerator counts how many such units are selected. Fractions must refer to the same whole before their quantities can be compared. Equivalent fractions represent the same quantity: multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer changes the partition without changing the quantity. For example, 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. To add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole, use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Adding the denominators gives the wrong unit. For positive addends, the sum should be greater than either addend; here it is also less than one whole. A counterexample guards the same-whole condition: half of a small cake need not equal half of a large cake. A drawn model should label the whole and show equal-sized parts. If the original wholes differ, first describe their sizes instead of treating the fractions alone as a sufficient comparison. Check a proposed answer by converting it back into the original quantities. A correct numerical answer with an unexplained unit still needs a reasoning check. Explain what the numerator counts and what unit the denominator names before applying a rule.

lesson.title: Counting Equal Parts and Building Sixths
lesson.objective: State that fractions describe selected equal parts of the same whole, name the denominator as the unit and the numerator as the count, apply the positive-integer equivalence rule, and add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole as 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
lesson.introduction: Fractions describe parts of one whole. To compare or add them, first make sure they refer to the same whole. Then name the unit and the count before applying a rule.
lesson.concept: A fraction describes selected equal parts of one whole. The denominator names the unit, and the numerator counts how many such units are selected. Before comparing fraction quantities, make sure they refer to the same whole. Equivalent fractions represent the same quantity: multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer changes the partition but not the quantity, for example 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. For 1/2 + 1/3 of the same whole, use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Adding the denominators gives the wrong unit. For positive addends, the sum should exceed either addend; this sum is also less than one whole. If the original wholes differ, describe their sizes first. The given chunk does not restrict denominators, and its page attribution is unchecked.
notes: Same whole first: compare quantities only then.

example.scenario: Use one whole. Add 1/2 and 1/3 of that same whole, then check the unit.
steps: Confirm both fractions refer to the same whole.
Name the units: halves and thirds are different units.
Check that 5/6 exceeds either addend and is less than one whole.
If the wholes differ, describe their sizes first.
example.conclusion: With the same whole, 1/2 + 1/3 becomes 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. The denominator names sixths; the numerator counts selected sixths.

misconception.claim: A correct numerical answer is enough even if the unit is unexplained.
misconception.correction: A correct numerical answer with an unexplained unit still needs a reasoning check. Explain what the numerator counts and what unit the denominator names before applying a rule.
board: Check the unit, not just the number

lesson.transfer: When a new task gives two wholes, do not compare or add the fractions until you confirm the wholes are the same. Name each unit, choose a common partition when needed, and check the result against the positive-addend expectation. If the wholes differ, describe their sizes instead of treating the fractions alone as sufficient.
lesson.summary: Fractions are selected equal parts of the same whole. The denominator names the unit; the numerator counts selected units. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same positive integer preserves quantity. With the same whole, 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
takeaways: Fractions need the same whole before comparison.
Denominator names the unit; numerator counts units.
Use the same positive multiplier for equivalence.

questions.prompt: Before comparing two fraction quantities, what condition does the source require?
options: They must refer to the same whole.
They must have the same numerator.
They must each be less than one.
questions.explanation: The source states that fractions must refer to the same whole before their quantities can be compared.
hints: Look for the condition tied to comparing quantities.
The condition concerns the whole, not the numerator.

questions.prompt: In the fraction 3/6, what does the denominator 6 name?
options: The size of the original whole
questions.explanation: The denominator names the unit, while the numerator counts how many selected units there are.
hints: Separate the naming role from the counting role.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly adds 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole by using sixths?
questions.explanation: Using sixths gives 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the sum is 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
hints: Rewrite each fraction with the same unit first.

questions.prompt: Which operation uses the positive-integer equivalence rule described in the source?
options: Add the same number to numerator and denominator.
Multiply numerator and denominator by different positive integers.
Multiply only the denominator by a positive integer.
Multiply both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer.
questions.explanation: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer changes the partition without changing the quantity.
hints: Look for the operation applied to both parts.
The multiplier must be positive and the same.
